questions: What changes - and what stays the same - as the dial turns from 300 K to 600 K?
Is the jiggle of one molecule the temperature, or is it something about all of them?
segments.say: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Watch the same four molecules as the dial turns from 300 K through 450 K to 600 K: the box does not change, the molecules do not change - their jiggle, on average, grows. Tell your partner: what exactly does the kelvin temperature measure?
segments.watchFor: Students who say the molecules themselves get bigger or multiply when heated. The count and the size never change; only the average kinetic energy rises.

questions: Does any single atom travel the length of the rod?
Why do metals conduct so much faster than wood?
segments.say: Conduction: heat travels atom by atom. Follow the energy packet down the rod - the hot atoms jiggle hard, bump their neighbours, and the jiggle relays along. In a metal, free electrons sprint the energy ahead of the lattice vibrations, which is why a metal rod warms at the far end long before a wooden one.
segments.watchFor: Students who picture heat as a fluid flowing through the rod. There is no substance flowing: only kinetic energy is passed from particle to particle.

questions: Why does the warmed parcel rise instead of staying at the heater?
Could convection happen in a solid? Why not?
segments.say: Convection: the fluid loops. The heater warms the fluid touching it, the warmed fluid expands and grows less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place. Trace one parcel all the way round - up the warm side, across, and down the cool side.

questions: What two things change about the packets when the filament goes from 300 K to 600 K?
Doubling the temperature multiplies the power by 16 - where does 16 come from?
segments.say: Radiation: hotter means more packets, faster. Every body radiates - watch even the cool body send out its one slow packet - and the Stefan-Boltzmann law P = sigma A T^4 says doubling the kelvin temperature multiplies the power by two to the fourth, sixteen times. No medium is needed: this is how the Sun warms the Earth across empty space.

questions: The cup is at 80 degrees and the bucket at 30 degrees: which has the higher temperature, and which holds more heat?
What is the difference between an average and a total here?
segments.say: Here is the trap, sprung on purpose: temperature is the average, heat is the total - the small hot cup wins on temperature, the big warm bucket wins on total heat. Now work through the worksheet in pairs, checking each answer against the trap section of your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: if you can explain why a hotter gas still has slow molecules, you have cracked today's lesson.
segments.watchFor: In a hotter gas every molecule moves faster. Listen for students who say exactly this when they explain heating. Send them back to the spread of speeds: the average shifts up, the spread remains, and some molecules still crawl.
